name: auto-scaling
context: Workload capacity must track demand instead of being fixed in advance. An automated control loop observes a metric — CPU or memory utilisation, a custom or per-pod metric, an external signal such as queue depth or QPS, or cluster size — and adjusts the deployed capacity to hold a target value: replica count horizontally, or per-instance resources vertically. In Kubernetes this is explicit and disaggregated: the HorizontalPodAutoscaler is a control-plane controller that periodically (default sync period 15s) reads metrics and writes the scale subresource of a Deployment or StatefulSet, applying scaling policies and a stabilization window so transient metric swings do not cause flapping; node autoscalers such as Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter separately provision and consolidate capacity for pods that cannot be scheduled; event-driven scaling is delegated to KEDA, which watches a message broker or other event source and drives the HPA, including scale-to-zero when no events are pending. Correctness hinges on declared resource requests — the HPA computes utilisation as a percentage of the request, so an unset request makes the metric meaningless.
benefits: Capacity matched to real demand, so a service can absorb traffic spikes without pre-provisioning for the worst case
Cost proportionality: nodes are provisioned when pods are unschedulable and consolidated when underutilised, so capacity is paid for only while it is needed
Removal of human scale-up latency — no ticket, no approval, no waiting for someone to notice the queue growing
Elastic handling of diurnal and event-driven load without resizing the fleet by hand
Per-workload policies: scale-up and scale-down can have different policies, stabilization windows and tolerances, since reacting to growth and shrinking is not symmetric
Metric flexibility beyond CPU — external metrics, per-pod metrics and event counts allow scaling on the resource that actually reflects demand
Scale to zero for spiky, intermittently used workloads where paying for idle capacity is the dominant cost
tradeoffs: Scaling is not instant: pod start-up, image pull, readiness probes and warm-up mean the autoscaler always reacts behind the spike, so it protects sustained load, not a sudden thundering herd
Good autoscaling depends entirely on good resource requests; wrong or missing requests produce oscillation or a fleet that scales far past the real need
Flapping risk when reacting to noisy or lagging metrics, mitigated only by stabilization windows and tolerance values that are themselves tuning

Vertical scaling and horizontal scaling are different mechanics with different failure modes — the HPA changes replica counts, the VPA changes requests and limits, and combining them naively can fight each other
Scaling a stateful workload means the new replicas need to catch up on state before serving, so scale-out latency is dominated by data movement
Cost unpredictability: an unbounded autoscaler reacting to a runaway loop can scale to the configured maximum at maximum speed
Metric plumbing is a real dependency — the resource metrics API, Metrics Server, Prometheus Adapter or KEDA must be installed and correct
use_cases: A payments API scaling pods on CPU to absorb a promotion-driven spike, with separate fast scale-up and conservative scale-down policies
Queue consumers sized by backlog depth using KEDA on Kafka or RabbitMQ, scaling to zero overnight and back to a full fleet on the first message
Node autoscaling provisioning capacity when pods go Pending and consolidating idle nodes to keep utilisation and cost balanced
A stateless HTTP service holding average CPU at 70% so latency stays flat as request volume doubles
Cluster-proportional autoscaling of system components such as cluster DNS so they track node count
Cron-scheduled autoscaling that pre-warms capacity ahead of a known daily batch window
avoid_when: Demand is genuinely fixed and predictable — autoscaling adds machinery and tuning surface for no gain
The latency budget cannot absorb pod start-up and readiness delay
Hard real-time or embedded targets where deterministic capacity must exist before the load arrives
Resource requests are unknown or unset, making the utilisation metric the autoscaler depends on meaningless
The state required to serve a request is expensive to move, so new replicas are useless for the minutes they need to catch up
Cost predictability matters more than elasticity and no spending ceiling is enforced
component_types: Autoscaler controller: the HPA in the control plane, evaluating metrics on a sync period
Metrics source: resource metrics API, custom.metrics.k8s.io, external.metrics.k8s.io, or Metrics Server as the provider
Scale target: a Deployment, StatefulSet or other resource exposing the scale subresource
Scaling policy and stabilization window: rate limits and smoothing rules for scale-up and scale-down
Node autoscaler: Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter, provisioning and consolidating nodes
Event-driven scaler: KEDA ScaledObject and its scalers bridging event sources to the HPA
Vertical Pod Autoscaler: adjusts container resource requests and limits
Budget guardrail: maximum replica count and cloud-level spend limits bounding runaway scaling
anti_patterns: No resource requests: the HPA divides observed usage by the request, so a missing request produces a meaningless ratio and erratic scaling
CPU-only scaling on I/O-bound services, which react to the wrong signal and scale on the wrong axis
Aggressive scale-down policies paired with aggressive scale-up: the fleet thrashes between states and pays pod start-up repeatedly
Multiple autoscalers writing to the same scale subresource, causing a fight over the replica count
No maximum: an autoscaler with an unbounded target turns a retry storm into a cost incident
Autoscaling a stateful workload while ignoring data movement latency, so new replicas join the load before they can serve it
Scaling on a metric with no relationship to demand — queue depth is right for a consumer, wrong for a synchronous API
design_principles: Capacity is a control loop, not a configuration value: observe, compute a desired replica count, write it, repeat
Respond to the bottleneck, not to CPU by default: the metric must be the one that actually limits throughput for that workload
Asymmetric policies: growth should be aggressive and shrinkage conservative, because the cost of under-provisioning is downtime and the cost of over-provisioning is money
Smoothing over instant reaction: stabilization windows and tolerances exist because metric noise must not translate into replica churn
Explicit resource requests as the contract between the workload and the autoscaler
Bounds everywhere: max replicas, per-workload ceilings and cost guardrails turn an unbounded loop into a predictable one
best_practices: Always declare CPU and memory requests — without them the HPA target is not computable in a meaningful way
Use autoscaling/v2 and define separate behavior.scaleUp and behavior.scaleDown policies rather than relying on defaults
Set a stabilization window on scale-down (Kubernetes defaults to 300s) so brief dips do not tear down capacity you will immediately need
Choose the metric that reflects the bottleneck: queue depth or QPS for I/O and event-driven work, CPU for compute-bound work
Use KEDA when the scaling signal is an event source, and set minReplicas to 0 with an object or external metric to reach true scale-to-zero
Pair horizontal workload autoscaling with node autoscaling, and set correct requests so the node autoscaler can place pods without surprise
Combine the HPA with the VPA to keep requests accurate as real usage diverges from the initial guess
Test scale-out latency end to end and verify warm-up time fits the load profile you expect
sources: KEDA, Scaling Deployments, StatefulSets and Custom Resources, https://keda.sh/docs/2.17/concepts/scaling-deployments/
